rationale: B wins because it turns the same facts into sharper editorial conflict without padding, especially "Klarna's AI did the work of 700 agents. It won't say how many people lost their jobs." A has the ingredients, but "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" crosses from advocate concern into an unproven decision claim. B still has a bruise in "AI-shrunk cost base," but its questions and next step are cleaner for a founder who has to survive the first reporter callback.
gaps_in_A: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" overstates the facts. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that the chatbot decides them.

"A profitable, IPO-bound Klarna leans on AI it won't fully explain" blurs the actual disclosure gap. Klarna won't break down cuts versus unfilled roles; the update does not say it refuses to explain the AI itself.

"Klarna cut average chat resolution from 11 minutes to under 2 — here's how" promises a process story the supplied facts cannot yet support. The set knows this, then asks for the missing mechanics in proof.
"regulator/advocate protagonist" sneaks in regulators where the update only gives consumer advocates. Do not conjure a regulator just because the beat would like one.
gaps_in_B: "AI-shrunk cost base" infers both cost-base movement and AI causality. The facts give profitability, a hiring freeze, and headcount down about 20%; they do not give cost data or the causal split.
"a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" is hedged, but "rule" still drags the dispute angle toward an unproven decision claim.
"The reporter will write this story with or without Klarna" is useful pressure, but it is bravado without evidence of an active reporter or live story.

"whether any of the displaced work was outsourced rather than in-house" is a fair proof question, but it introduces a new possible explanation that is not in the fact block and should stay clearly framed as a question.
